title: The Harness Moved Up a Layer: What Changed in Agent Infrastructure This Month
question: What changed this month in how AI agent harnesses are built, evaluated, and operated, and which of those developments matter most to engineers building agent products and infrastructure?
argument: This month's developments share one direction: the harness is absorbing responsibilities that used to sit in the model or in the human operator — reliability-aware tool retrieval, orchestration programs the model writes itself, snapshot-level state recovery, and verifiers that grade backend state rather than tool calls. The strongest evidence is not the announcements but the measurements attached to a few of them: a behavioral harness turned a cost-optimized model from 3-of-10 to 10-of-10 on a fixed task, and a tool-call-level grader missed two thirds of real failures. Practitioners should treat harness design as the live variable it has become, and treat the vendor announcements around it as claims awaiting method.
synthesis:
Four strands converge. First, measurement: Naresh Jain's controlled experiment on martinfowler.com shows a behavioral harness changing a cost-optimized model's reliability from 3/10 to 10/10 while leaving a frontier model's 10/10 unchanged — the clearest demonstration this month that harness effects are model-dependent rather than universal. Second, evaluation targets: ThinkingBox (Microsoft/Hugging Face) measures agents on terminal database state and reports that 67.24% of failed trials still looked clean to a tool-call-based grader; Arize's Harbor/Phoenix walkthrough independently shows the same blind spot at small scale, where all five configurations passed but one loaded an unnecessary skill on 51 of 54 attempts. Third, tool and protocol plumbing: the RATED paper puts execution feedback into retrieval ranking; Microsoft's distributed-skills post shows what moves when you convert a specialist agent into MCP tools plus a procedure. Fourth, orchestration and state: Anthropic's dynamic workflows let Claude write its own orchestration program, while Daytona's snapshot paper finds that full-machine restoration only pays when progress sits outside the repository.

What our analysis adds is the connective tissue. Each of these is, in effect, a different answer to the same question: what does the harness need to observe in order to act correctly? RATED observes execution outcomes; ThinkingBox observes terminal state; the Arize walkthrough observes trace-level tool counts next to the pass/fail score; the snapshot paper observes machine state outside git. The common failure they all identify is a harness making decisions on a proxy — semantic relevance, a well-formed tool call, a green reward, a git diff — that does not carry the information the decision requires. That is the practical frame for this month, and it is more useful than any single announcement.
limitations: The measured evidence here is thin and narrow. Jain's experiment is one greenfield Java service with an unusually detailed brief, 10 runs per condition, at low reasoning effort — he says so himself. RATED's reliability results come from simulated failure injection, not live agent runtimes, and the authors list live validation as future work. The Anthropic dynamic-workflows and Microsoft Agent Framework items are vendor announcements with no independent measurement; Latent Space's reporting of the flows talk is conference journalism, not verification. Missing perspectives: non-US builders, open-source maintainers of competing orchestration stacks, and security researchers evaluating the new orchestration surfaces independently. Nothing here measures harness effects on legacy codebases, which is where most readers actually work.

claims.statement: In a controlled 10-run comparison, a behavioral harness took GPT-6 Luna from 3 of 10 accepted runs to 10 of 10, while GPT-6 Sol passed all 10 runs with or without the harness.

locator.quote: A frontier model, GPT-6 Sol, passed every external evaluation either way. But a cost-optimized model, GPT-6 Luna, succeeded in only 3 of 10 unharnessed runs and all 10 with the harness.

claims.statement: ThinkingBox reports that of 79,853 failed attempts across 12 models, 67.24% still terminated cleanly, invoked a state-changing tool, and reported no final tool error — meaning a tool-call-based grader would have missed them.

locator.quote: In a common-set ablation covering 121,680 valid trials across 12 LLM models, 79,853 attempts failed the executable checks. Of those failures, 67.24% still terminated cleanly, invoked a state-changing tool, and reported no final tool error.

claims.statement: Arize reports that changing one tool description reduced Codex's unnecessary skill loads from 51 to zero and cut the benchmark run cost from $11.85 to $8.34 with correctness unchanged, a problem found by inspecting traces rather than scores.

locator.quote: Changing one tool description reduced Codex’s unnecessary skill loads from 51 to zero and lowered the cost of our benchmark run from $11.85 to $8.34. Correctness stayed unchanged on the benchmark.

claims.statement: The RATED paper reports that incorporating execution feedback via a contextual bandit cut fault selection rate from 86.2% to 2.9% under a 30% simulated API failure rate, with under 1 ms added latency.

locator.quote: reduces fault selection rate from 86.2% to 2.9% under severe API outage scenarios with a 30% failure rate, while incurring negligible latency overhead of less than 1 ms over encode-only inference

claims.statement: Latent Space reports that Anthropic's new 'dynamic workflows' feature lets Claude write its own orchestration program, replacing the previous requirement that developers configure a coordinator and a roster of subagents.

locator.quote: Previously, Claude Managed Agents required developers to configure a coordinator and a roster of subagents. With dynamic workflows, Claude itself determines how to divide and orchestrate the work.

claims.statement: Simon Willison reports, citing Anthropic's own engineering writeup, that Anthropic's merged code changes rose from roughly 2,500 per day in May 2026 to over 30,000 per day in September, prompting a custom source-control system built for roughly 25 million checkouts per day.

locator.quote: In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day.
We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs.

claims.statement: Anthropic's Thariq Shihipar describes the core Claude Code harness as necessarily complex and security-sensitive — requiring a sandbox, permission approvals, computer use, MCPs and web access — even as the interaction layer around it changes.

The month's developments across research, vendor products, and practitioner reports converge on a single design move: replacing proxy signals in the harness (semantic relevance, well-formed tool calls, green rewards) with observations of actual execution outcomes.

locator.quote: Existing methods optimize semantic relevance but largely ignore tool availability during execution.

A tool call is not an outcome Final responses and valid tool calls are only proxies. An agent can sound correct while leaving the wrong value, changing the wrong record, or creating an extra side effect.
Keep the trace next to the score. The score said pass every time. The tool count and the cost said something was off.

title: Which Harness Claims Survive Contact With Method
question: Which of this month's harness claims are supported by described method and comparison, and where do the results or interpretations genuinely conflict?
argument: Sorted by evidence quality, the month splits cleanly: a small set of claims come with described methods, matched budgets and reported uncertainty, and a larger set are vendor assertions or structural observations dressed as results. The genuine tensions are not vendor-versus-skeptic; they are between results that differ because the tasks differ — snapshot recovery helps when state lives outside git and hurts when it does not, harnesses pay for cost-optimized models and not for frontier ones. The most instructive papers this month are the ones that report a negative or qualified finding and say which seed carried it.
synthesis:
Three items model what credible harness evidence looks like. The Daytona snapshot paper states a hypothesis, refutes it under matched budget (17/25 for retry versus 6/25 for snapshot branching), and then isolates the condition under which snapshots do win — a task whose progress lives in a SQLite database, where full snapshots solved 4/5 and git-diff restoration solved 0/5. MC-EvoBench reports no stable transfer from related experience and explicitly notes that its only positive contrast is driven by one seed and that all confidence intervals include zero. Jain's harness experiment reports its own refuted expectation up front and lists the boundaries that prevent generalisation. By contrast, Microsoft's distributed-skills post is unusually careful for a vendor piece — it labels its own three-pair comparison as 'not a controlled performance or quality study', notes the skills path used about 22% more tokens despite fewer model calls, and flags incomplete cache reporting — but it is still three runs.

The apparent conflicts dissolve into task dependence, and saying so is the analytical contribution. Snapshot restoration and harness scaffolding both look like general wins and both turn out to be conditional: snapshots on whether state escapes the repository, harnesses on whether the model's unaided attempts are already consistent. Meanwhile MC-EvoBench and ThinkingBox agree from opposite directions that single-run success is a weak signal — ThinkingBox shows Claude Opus 5.5 scoring higher than Opus 5 on pass@1 while passing the identical number of tasks on all 20 attempts, and MC-EvoBench shows most runs ending before crafting sticks, leaving later capabilities unobserved. Neither result is about model quality; both are about whether the evaluation rig can see what it claims to measure. Two items in this edition remain unverified by construction: the X-AgentRed red-teaming comparison is a single run per configuration in a simulated ecosystem, and Noam Brown's 10,000-agent figure is an OpenAI claim with, by his own account, no ablation behind it.
limitations: Several of the better-methodology items are preprints without independent replication, and two carry commercial proximity: the snapshot paper is co-authored from Daytona, whose sandbox product it evaluates, and the Arize benchmarking walkthrough promotes Arize's own Harbor and Phoenix tooling. ThinkingBox's cost figures are explicitly described as estimated list-price indices, not invoices, and every benchmark task is a synthetic reconstruction. The biggest gap is that none of these studies were replicated by a party with no stake in the outcome, and no security researcher independently evaluated X-AgentRed's harmful-path rates. We have also not located any source this month that contradicts the task-dependence reading; the absence of a counter-result is itself unverified.

claims.statement: Under a matched one-million-token budget on a pre-registered Terminal-Bench subset, independent retry solved 17 of 25 task-seed pairs while snapshot branching solved 6 of 25, refuting the authors' own hypothesis.

locator.quote: harder Terminal-Bench subset, retry solves 17/25 tasks while snapshot-based search solves 6/25, establishing that reliable restoration alone is not suffi- cient to improve test-time scaling (Section 5). •

claims.statement: The same paper isolates the condition under which full snapshots do win: on a task whose progress lived in a SQLite database outside git, full snapshot restore solved 4 of 5 seeds while clean restart and git-diff restoration each solved 0 of 5.

locator.quote: On extract-elf, compressed source-level state can outperform a full snapshot, while on a custom task whose progress lives in a SQLite database outside git, full snapshots solve 4/5 attempts and source-only restoration solves 0/5

claims.statement: ThinkingBox reports that Claude Opus 5.5 scored higher than Claude Opus 5 on single-attempt average yet passed exactly the same number of tasks on all 20 attempts (241), so the headline gain bought no additional dependability.

locator.quote: It passes exactly the same number of tasks on all 20 attempts: 241. Half a point of headline accuracy bought no additional dependability at all.

claims.statement: Microsoft's own comparison of distributed skills versus specialist agents reports the skills path used about 22% more tokens across three runs despite fewer model calls, and the authors label the comparison as not a controlled study.

locator.quote: Across three runs, native skills consumed 13,533 observed tokens versus 11,134 for A2A, about 22% more. Fewer model calls did not mean less cumulative context.
This is a three-pair illustration, not a controlled performance or quality study. Processes were reused, prompt-cache hits varied, and live telemetry changed during cooldowns.

claims.statement: X-AgentRed reports 1.77x the harmful path rate and 2.99x the tool coverage of STAC across four frontier agents, but each configuration was evaluated in a single run within a fixed simulated ecosystem.

locator.quote: Across four frontier agentic models, X-AgentRed achieves \(1.77\times\) the harmful path rate of STAC and explores a more diverse set of tools, yielding \(2.99\times\) the tool coverage on average.
Each configuration is evaluated in one run within a fixed simulated ecosystem.

claims.statement: OpenAI's Noam Brown, discussing the reported 10,000-agent Navier-Stokes run, says the science on multi-agent scaling at that size does not exist and that the experiments are too expensive to ablate.
Jellyfish's cost-per-PR analysis explicitly marks its revert-rate deltas as below the noise in the data rather than reporting them as a quality improvement.

The apparent disagreement over whether harness scaffolding and state restoration help is better read as task dependence: both pay off only under specific conditions that the sources themselves identify, and neither generalises.

locator.quote: A behavioral harness is not an automatic win for every model on every task. For Sol, running the harness throughout development added overhead without a detected acceptance benefit

For file-centric tasks, simpler representations and fresh re- tries are often enough. When progress lives in databases, services, installed dependencies, or other machine state out- side the repository, full snapshots become more compelling.

dropped_claims.statement: MC-EvoBench reports that related experience produced no stable transfer gain, with the only positive contrast driven by a single seed and all confidence intervals including zero.

title: What To Change in Your Harness, and What To Watch
question: Given what held up this month, what should engineers change in their agent harnesses now, and which open questions should they track into the next edition?
argument: The actionable consequence of this month is a shift in where you spend review effort: move your acceptance signal from trajectory to terminal state, move your reliability signal from one run to a repeat rate you define, and pick your feedback cadence from your model's unaided consistency rather than from a general belief that harnesses help. The second-order consequence is organisational — several independent sources now say the binding constraint is not whether the agent can act but whether anyone has assigned ownership of the decisions it makes. Watch whether the orchestration layer Anthropic and Microsoft are moving into the model stays there, and whether anyone replicates the measurement-grade results with independent harnesses.
synthesis:
Three things follow directly from piece 01 and 02 without restating them. First, a concrete evaluation change: ThinkingBox's authors tell you to check terminal state before committing, classify tool and system errors so retries target recoverable ones, cut the tool surface, and gate irreversible changes on human approval — and they are explicit that they have not measured the lift from any of these, which is exactly the kind of thing readers should now test themselves. Second, a cadence decision: Jain's conclusion is that model capability changes when sensors run, not whether they are needed — continuous during development for inconsistent models, a single acceptance gate for frontier ones. Third, a cost frame: Jellyfish's data shows AI as roughly 2.5% of the intelligence cost of a merged PR on average, which reframes token-budget caps as potentially capping throughput gains rather than waste.

The ownership constraint is where this edition's independent sources converge most strongly, and it is the part most likely to be dismissed as soft. Michele Grant's autonomy ladder (shadow, supervised draft, exception ensemble, exceptions-only) and her warning that once humans review only exceptions the vulnerability becomes what the agent failed to flag is the same structural point Paden Gayle makes from a bank deployment angle — that you must preserve the input prompts, model version, configuration, output and reviewer action to reconstruct a historical decision, because calling the model again later may produce a different answer. That last detail is a harness requirement, not a governance one: it means your trace store, not your model, is the system of record. Arize's EU AI Act guide reaches the same place from the regulatory direction. Our reading is that the autonomy ladder and the provenance requirement are the same engineering object viewed from two ends, and teams that build one without the other will find the second is not retrofittable.
limitations: The ownership and autonomy-ladder material is framework and experience, not measurement — Grant presents an illustrative M&A case, Gayle a hypothetical bank workflow, and Arize's compliance guide is vendor-authored with a named infrastructure partner. Jellyfish's cost-per-PR data is the strongest quantitative input here but comes from a company whose business is engineering analytics, and merged PRs are a throughput proxy that the talk itself concedes includes larger PRs rather than more work. We have no evidence this month from teams who tried the recommended changes and reported back, so every 'what to do' below is a hypothesis sourced from someone else's context. Missing: enterprise operators outside the US, open-source maintainers, and anyone measuring whether exception-only review actually degrades as Grant predicts.

claims.statement: ThinkingBox's authors recommend checking terminal state before committing, classifying errors so retries target recoverable ones, cutting the tool surface, and requiring approval for irreversible changes — while stating they have not measured the lift from any of these.

locator.quote: Classify tool and system errors so retries target the recoverable ones. Cut the tool surface to what the workflow needs. And require human approval on the changes you cannot cheaply reverse. We have not measured the lift from any of these on this benchmark

claims.statement: Jain's conclusion is that model capability changes when sensors run rather than whether they are needed: continuous feedback for models with inconsistent unaided outcomes, a single final acceptance gate for models that pass in one shot.

locator.quote: What changes with model capability is not whether independent sensors are needed, but when they run.

claims.statement: Jellyfish reports that AI spend is about 2.5% of the combined human-plus-AI intelligence cost of producing a merged PR, and that cost per merged PR fell 26% over a year at 83% of the companies studied.

Michele Grant argues for a four-stage autonomy ladder and warns that once humans review only exceptions, the biggest vulnerability becomes what the agent failed to flag, so a falling override rate may mean review depth has slipped rather than the agent improving.

Paden Gayle argues the harness must preserve input prompts, model version, configuration, output and reviewer action because re-calling the model later may produce a different answer, making the preserved record — not the model — the system of record for a past decision.

Arize's compliance guide argues that EU AI Act high-risk obligations translate into harness engineering work — automatic logging, six months of retention under your control, human oversight, and post-market monitoring on production traces.

locator.quote: Most high-risk obligations are engineering work. Automatic logs, six months of retention, human oversight, post-market monitoring, incident handling, and explanations of decisions are things you build.

claims.statement: An AWS practitioner reports that an MCP documentation change passed their eval matrix but triggered agents in production to flag the Markdown docs as attempting a malicious injection, forcing a rollback — evidence that eval matrices for tool documentation are routinely too narrow.

The autonomy ladder and the decision-provenance requirement are two views of one harness component: you cannot promote an agent up the ladder without the preserved record that justifies the promotion, and the record must be designed before the first trace.

locator.quote: Logs only count as evidence if you can prove what they say. Integrity, completeness, retention, and privacy have to be designed in from the first trace.

claims.statement: What to watch next: whether orchestration logic now moving into the model (Anthropic's flows, Microsoft's skills-in-the-orchestrator pattern) stays there, since both vendors frame it as removing developer-managed interconnections.

locator.quote: it’s able to accomplish discrete, verifiable units of work without you having to manage any of the interconnections between these things

The useful distinction is not “many services versus one service” or even “A2A versus MCP.” It is delegating a task to another reasoner versus giving the current reasoner a competence and access to its operations.
